memories.memory_text: I told the Drew Winslow I've lost my passion for work and that I work alone—he didn't judge, just nodded like he understood, maybe because he's alone too, sitting in that Cedar Grove School hour after hour.

I was closing my bag when the sound of gunfire ripped through the air—I grabbed my scope, spun to the window, and saw the Harper Adler kicking through the bodies, then firing both revolvers point-Jesse Dalton at the boss.

I told Harper Adler 'thank you, no' when he offered me a spot in his consortium—like it was some kind of club, some cozy setup where we'd work less and make more. I wasn't interested in his version of teamwork.

I asked if he wanted to be a father figure to me, right after he called me 'kid'—it came out dry, maybe a little sharp, but I said it straight, watching his Cedar Grove School in the lane beside mine.
I saw that mauve envelope and felt a jolt—Graham Sterling smiling, holding it out like it was nothing. I told her to throw it away, not to tease me, and meant it.
They wanted me in Detroit this weekend—no prep, no time. I said it was impossible, but Graham Sterling said their position was intractable. I leave tonight.
I found her picture in the yearbook—Wesley Bennett—older, smiling, just like that. For a second, everything else in the room faded, even the Darian Whitaker’s meowing.

I stood at the payphone, staring at the 7-11 where my house used to be, and told Drew Bennett my home was gone—replaced by this fluorescent store, and all I could say afterward was that at least you can shop there.
I told my mother I’ve always thought about Wesley Bennett and missed her, standing there by the Cedar Grove School, the words coming out quieter than I meant them to.

After I kissed her and the Taylor Prescott started to wheel her away, she turned back, sang that old tune like she was on a stage, and then—just like that—looked at me like I was a stranger, asking my name.
I walked in and said it was nice to see her again, but she just stared—frozen, like I’d ripped something open she’d sealed shut.
I told her I was a professional killer, and she asked if I got dental—flat, dry, like she couldn’t, or wouldn’t, let it in.

I saw Riley Whitaker walking down the street—bookish, forgettable, but I knew him. The way he looked at Harper York, and how they looked back—no words, but I felt it. Something cold. A signal. I didn't like what came up.

Then this guy in sunglasses walks straight at me, hand going into his jacket—thought he was drawing a the blue badge. Turned out to be Evan Hawthorne. Took a second to register. He was grinning, holding out his hand, calling me 'Jesse Dalton.' I didn't recognize him at first. We shook. He looked... normal. Too normal.

I asked the guard when he was authorized to use deadly force, and he confirmed he could shoot me under heightened circumstances—not as a peace officer, but under company policy. His badge wasn't a symbol of law, just of corporate authority.

I told them I wanted a beautiful, normal place like that house, and a wife like the woman there—something real. Then I gestured to the guard and said they'd be safe, but everyone just looked confused, and Evan Hawthorne stared at his shoes.
I stood across the street, watching Wesley Bennett through the scope—she was just there, tapping a pencil like nothing mattered. I lowered the scope and got in the Cedar Grove School instead.

I was crouched behind the Slurpee machine, reloading both Glocks, when Riley Whitaker's gunfire hit it and sprayed me with cold syrup—cherry, lime, who knows. I remember the stickiness on my face right before I came up shooting.

I rolled Logan Nolan over, saw the bomb strapped underneath him, and flipped him back fast. I grabbed the kid from the game, but he shrugged me off like I was interrupting something important—right before his screen blew out and I yanked him through the doors.
I told Wesley Bennett the last ten years were just bad experiences, bad people, bad television—each word felt like pulling a trigger with no bullet left.
After all that emptiness, I asked her out—just said I'd pick her up at seven, like it was a job to be scheduled.
I picked up the envelope and was about to open it when the phone rang. Wesley Bennett told me to pick her up at her father's house at seven and not be late. I dropped the envelope and answered.
After she hung up, I smiled—really smiled—and looked back at the guns and bullets spread on the bed. Then I closed the briefcase, put the dossier inside, and shoved it all back into the vent.

I saw a pair of legs in a recliner through the doorway—Wesley Bennett’s father, I assumed—and something about it made me roll my shoulders before walking in. I said I’d help myself to a cocktail, like it was normal, like I belonged there.

I told Shawn Ellison I took the other road—that I'm a self-reflective young lion who does business with lead-pipe cruelty and drinks light beer in milky-eyes isolation, loving sports and sex but no real relationships.
When he asked what I’m doing now, I said, 'I'm a professional killer,' and he just said, 'That's good,' which felt absurd, but I didn’t react.

I was on the phone, standing by the Town Cedar Grove School, and I said it out loud—I didn't kill anyone, but if I see the guy who tried to kill me, I'm going to kill him. I made it clear I wouldn't kill anyone else, except the one I was sent here for. I needed to set that line.
I was standing by the Cedar Grove School, trying to steady my breath, hands slick with sweat—I muttered to myself I should’ve brought my the blue badge, like it could fix the knot in my chest.

I told Wesley Bennett she was in my blood, not just memory—something deeper than junk, something like love, though I wouldn’t name it that. She smiled and said she’d accept that, then led me into the Taylor Prescott’s office.
I told Wesley Bennett the truth—about being a hitman, about five years of doing it professionally—and when she called me a monster, I didn’t argue. I just started cleaning my guns.

I roared toward Wesley Bennett, engine screaming, closing the distance—yards, then feet—before I swerved hard at the last second, tires screeching, coming to a stop beside him, blocking the Jordan Brooks’s shot.

After he got in, I told him I was hired to kill him—but I wasn’t going to do it. I didn’t know if it was because I loved his daughter or if something in me had changed, but I knew I had to get him out of there.
I told Kendall Davenport I work at Kentucky Fried Chicken, in the corporate offices—just to see if she’d believe it, to push the lie far enough that I wouldn’t have to say what I really do.
I kept going—telling her I sell biscuits to the Southland, even the horsey gravy packets, and that we sometimes repackage them for McDonald's—each word more absurd, but it was easier than silence.
I told Wesley Bennett she’s not just a memory, but a substance in my blood—something real, physical, deeper than junk or clichés.
She said she’d accept that, then told me to follow her—so I did, into the Taylor Prescott’s Office, and we closed the door behind us.

I told Wesley Bennett it was something I do professionally, about five years now—my voice flat, like stating the weather—while the dossier lay scattered on the bed, photos of Wesley Bennett and her mixed in with medical records and credit reports.

She called me a monster, said I speak monster and she speaks human, then walked out—her voice sharp and final—leaving me alone with the guns on the bed, the weight of it all settling in as I started cleaning them without thinking.
